collisions-s2.title: Two carts that stick
collisions-s2.html: The track is level and friction is negligible. Positive is to the right.

items.q: What is cart 1's momentum? Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: that is ½mv. Momentum has no ½: p = mv.

items.q: How do the momenta and kinetic energies of the two carts compare?
options: Equal momenta; cart 2 has 4 times the kinetic energy
Equal momenta and equal kinetic energies
Cart 2 has 4 times the momentum and 4 times the kinetic energy
Cart 1 has more momentum, because it is heavier

items.q: Cart 2 reverses and moves left at 4.0 m/s. What is the momentum of the two-cart system now?
options: 4.0 kg·m/s to the right
Zero
2.0 kg·m/s to the right

items.q: What is the velocity of the center of mass of the two carts, both moving right as shown?
What is cart B's velocity after the carts separate, in m/s? Include the sign.

mistakes.why: Value: B moves the opposite way from A, to the right, so its velocity is positive.
Value: equal momenta, not equal speeds: B is lighter, so it moves faster.

items.q: What is the velocity of the two-cart system's center of mass after the carts separate?
options: +1.2 m/s, the faster cart's velocity
−0.80 m/s, the heavier cart's velocity
+0.40 m/s, the average of the two velocities
Zero

items.q: Which cart gets more kinetic energy from the spring?
options: B, the lighter cart
A, the heavier cart
Neither: they get equal kinetic energies
Neither: the total kinetic energy stays zero

items.q: Why can the spring's push be treated with the explosion model?
options: The spring's forces are external, so they do not change the momentum
Its forces are internal and briefly far larger than outside forces
The spring does no work on the carts, so the energy is unchanged
The carts have equal masses, so their speeds are equal and opposite

items.q: A 0.15 kg ball moving right at 20 m/s and a 1200 kg car moving left at 0.0025 m/s are compared. Which is true?
options: The car has far more momentum, because of its mass
The ball has far more momentum, because it is faster
Same size of momentum, opposite directions
Their momenta are equal, including direction

items.q: If an object's speed doubles, by what factor does its momentum change, and by what factor does its kinetic energy change?
options: Both ×2
Both ×4
Momentum ×4, kinetic energy ×2
Momentum ×2, kinetic energy ×4

items.q: A 0.50 kg cart has a momentum of 3.0 kg·m/s. What is its kinetic energy, in joules?

mistakes.why: Value: you left out the 2. From K = ½mv² and p = mv, K = p²/(2m).
Value: the momentum must be squared: K = p²/(2m).

items.q: A ball moving right at 5.0 m/s bounces straight back at 5.0 m/s. Which is true of its momentum and kinetic energy?
options: Its momentum changed; its kinetic energy did not
Neither changed, because the speed is the same
Both changed
Its kinetic energy changed; its momentum did not

items.q: A 70.0 kg skater moves at 3.0 m/s and a 50.0 kg skater moves at 4.2 m/s in the same direction. What is the momentum of the pair (the sum of their momenta), in kg·m/s?
A two-object system has a center of mass that moves at constant velocity. What can you conclude?
options: Both objects move at constant velocity
The net external force on the system is zero
The two objects exert no forces on each other
The system has no kinetic energy

items.q: Cart 1 (mass m) moves right at speed v. Cart 2 (mass 2m) moves right at speed v/2. Predict how each quantity for cart 2 compares with cart 1.
Which unit is the same as kg·m/s?
options: J
N
N·s
W

items.q: Use the graph to find the impulse the wall exerts on the ball. Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: that is the area of a rectangle. The graph is a triangle: area = ½ × base × height.
Value: the time is in milliseconds. 4 ms = 0.004 s.

items.q: What is the ball's change in momentum, in kg·m/s? Include the sign.

mistakes.why: Value: the initial velocity is to the left, so it is −4.0 m/s. Δp = m(v_f − v_i) = 0.20(2.0 − (−4.0)).

items.q: What is the average force of the wall on the ball during the 4.0 ms contact, in newtons?

mistakes.why: Value: 600 N is the peak force. The average over a triangle is half the peak: J/Δt.

items.q: A softer ball with the same mass and the same speeds before and after stays in contact for 8.0 ms instead. How does the wall's force compare?
options: Same impulse, half the average force
Twice the impulse, same average force
Same impulse, same average force
Half the impulse, half the average force

items.q: A clay ball of the same mass and speed hits the wall and sticks. How does the impulse on it compare with the bouncing ball's?
options: Larger, because the clay comes to a full stop
Smaller: 0.80 N·s instead of 1.2 N·s
The same, because the incoming momentum is the same
Zero, because the clay ends at rest

items.q: What is the net force on the cart between 0 and 3.0 s, in newtons?

mistakes.why: Value: that is the change in momentum. The net force is the slope: Δp/Δt.

items.q: What is the net force on the cart from 3.0 s to 5.0 s?
options: 1.2 N, the momentum value
0.40 N, the same as during the push
Zero, because the momentum is constant
Negative, because the cart is slowing

items.q: What is the cart's speed at 4.0 s, in m/s?

mistakes.why: Value: that multiplies by the mass. Divide instead: v = p/m.

items.q: Which graph of net force against time matches the momentum graph?
options: Rising from 0 to 1.2 N over 3.0 s, then constant
Zero from 0 to 3.0 s, then 1.2 N
A constant 0.40 N for the whole 5.0 s
0.40 N from 0 to 3.0 s, then zero

items.q: A tennis racket exerts an average force of 250 N on a ball for 0.0060 s. What impulse does it deliver, in N·s?

mistakes.why: Value: impulse is force times time, not force divided by time.

items.q: A 0.058 kg tennis ball arrives at 30. m/s and leaves the racket at 40. m/s in the opposite direction. What is the size of the impulse on the ball, in N·s?

mistakes.why: Value: you subtracted speeds. The velocities have opposite signs: Δv = 40 − (−30) = 70 m/s.

items.q: Why does bending your knees when you land from a jump reduce the force on your legs?
options: It lengthens the stopping time, so the same change in momentum needs a smaller average force
It reduces your change in momentum
It reduces your kinetic energy before landing
It reduces the impulse the ground gives you

items.q: The same average force acts on a cart for three times as long. The change in the cart's momentum becomes
options: 9 times as large
3 times as large
one third as large
the same

items.q: On a graph of force against time, what represents the impulse?
options: The slope of the curve
The highest force on the graph
The area under the curve
The time at which the force is largest

items.q: An egg dropped onto a pillow is compared with the same egg dropped from the same height onto a hard floor (where it stops sooner). Predict how each pillow value compares with the floor value.

variables.name: The average force on the egg

items.q: What is cart B's velocity after the collision, in m/s?

mistakes.why: Value: B does not simply take A's speed. Use momentum: (0.50)(0.80) = (0.50)(0.30) + (0.25)v_B.
Value: that is A's change in velocity. B's mass is half of A's, so B's change is twice as large.

items.q: Which is the best justification for using momentum conservation here?
options: The net external force on the two carts is zero: vertical forces balance and friction is negligible
Momentum is conserved because of the law of conservation of momentum, which holds for any collision
The carts exert equal forces on each other, so each cart's momentum is constant
Kinetic energy is conserved in the collision, so momentum is conserved as well

items.q: How does the impulse cart A exerts on cart B compare with the impulse cart B exerts on cart A?
options: B's impulse on A is larger, because A is heavier
Equal in size and opposite in direction
A's impulse on B is larger, because B speeds up more
Equal in size and in the same direction

items.q: Take cart A alone as the system. Which is correct?
options: A's momentum is constant, because the track is frictionless
A's momentum is constant, because the collision is brief
A's momentum is not constant, because B exerts an external force on it
A has no momentum after the collision, since its momentum went to B

items.q: How does the velocity of the center of mass of the two carts after the collision compare with before?
options: It increases, because B speeds up
It decreases, because A slows down
It is zero after the collision
It is the same, about +0.53 m/s

items.q: How fast do the dart and block move just after the dart sticks, in m/s?

mistakes.why: Value: after the collision the dart moves with the block. Divide by the total mass, 0.500 kg.
Value: that sets kinetic energies equal. The dart sticks, so kinetic energy is not conserved; use momentum.

items.q: Why can momentum, but not kinetic energy, be used to find the speed just after the dart sticks?
options: No net external force acts on them, but friction inside the block makes thermal energy
Kinetic energy is conserved as well, but the momentum equation is easier to solve
Momentum is conserved just for collisions where the objects join
The rough patch removes momentum but not kinetic energy

items.q: The dart and block then slide onto the rough patch. How far do they slide before stopping, in meters?

mistakes.why: Value: that uses the dart's speed. On the patch the dart and block move together at 4.0 m/s.

items.q: While the dart and block slide on the rough patch, is the momentum of the dart-block system constant?
options: Yes: momentum is conserved whatever the forces
No: friction from the patch is a net external force
Yes: the dart and the block move together as one object
No: the dart is now inside the block

items.q: A ball falls toward Earth. For which system is momentum constant (ignoring the rest of the universe)?
options: The ball alone
Earth alone
Ball + Earth
Neither the ball alone nor ball + Earth

items.q: A 60. kg skater at rest throws a 3.0 kg ball forward at 8.0 m/s on frictionless ice. What is the skater's recoil speed, in m/s?

mistakes.why: Value: the skater and ball separate, so the skater's mass alone (60. kg) carries the recoil.

items.q: An astronaut at rest throws a wrench away. If she throws a wrench of twice the mass at the same speed, her recoil speed becomes
options: 4 times as large
√2 times as large
the same
2 times as large

items.q: Two ice skaters push off each other from rest. Skater 1 has twice the mass of skater 2. Which statement is correct?
options: Skater 2 moves off twice as fast as skater 1, the other way
Both move away at the same speed, in opposite directions
Skater 1 moves away twice as fast, because skater 1 is bigger
Skater 1 does not move, because skater 2 does the pushing

items.q: A 1.5 kg cart moving right at 2.0 m/s collides with a 0.50 kg cart moving left at 3.0 m/s. After the collision the 0.50 kg cart moves right at 1.5 m/s. What is the 1.5 kg cart's velocity after, in m/s? Include the sign (right positive).

mistakes.why: Value: the 0.50 kg cart moves left before, so its momentum is negative: (0.50)(−3.0).

items.q: A moving cart collides with a cart at rest on a level, frictionless track. For the two-cart system, compare after with before.

variables.name: The velocity of the center of mass
The momentum of the cart that was moving

items.q: In which trials is the total momentum of the two carts the same before and after?
options: In each of the three trials
In trial 1, the elastic one, and not the others
In trial 3, where the carts stick, and not the others
In no trial, because the carts' speeds change

items.q: Which trial is elastic?
options: Trial 2
Trial 1
Trial 3
Each of the three, because momentum is conserved in each

items.q: How much kinetic energy is converted to other forms in trial 3, in joules?

mistakes.why: Value: that is the kinetic energy after. Subtract it from the 0.20 J before.

items.q: In trial 1, cart A bounces back. Did cart A's own kinetic energy stay the same?
options: Yes: in an elastic collision each cart keeps its kinetic energy
Yes: A moves back with its original speed
No: A gave most of its K to B; the total stayed 0.20 J
No: the total kinetic energy went down

items.q: Trial 3 is repeated with cart B loaded to 1.60 kg. Compared with the original trial 3, the speed of the stuck carts after the collision is
options: the same, because A has the same momentum
one quarter as large
twice as large
one half as large

items.q: What is the velocity of the stuck carts just after the collision, in m/s? Include the sign.

mistakes.why: Value: B moves left, so its momentum is negative: (1.0)(−1.5).
Value: averaging velocities ignores the masses. Use total momentum over total mass.

items.q: How much kinetic energy does the system lose in the collision, in joules?

mistakes.why: Value: kinetic energies do not cancel. B's 1.1 J adds to A's 9.0 J even though B moves left.

items.q: A student finds the final velocity by setting the kinetic energy before equal to the kinetic energy after. What is wrong?
options: K is not conserved when carts stick; start from momentum
Nothing: kinetic energy is conserved in a collision like this one
The student should have used the carts' weights instead of masses
Kinetic energy gives the speed but not the direction, so add a sign

items.q: Which momentum bar chart (bars for A, B and the total, before and after) is correct?
options: Before: A +6.0, B +1.5, total +7.5; after: total +7.5
Before: A +6.0, B −1.5, total +4.5; after: A and B together +4.5
Before: A +6.0, B −1.5, total +4.5; after: 0, because the carts stop
Before: A +3.0, B −1.5, total +1.5; after: +1.5

items.q: Which is true of every collision between two objects on a level, frictionless surface?
options: Total kinetic energy is conserved; momentum may or may not be
Both total momentum and total kinetic energy are conserved
Momentum is conserved; kinetic energy may or may not be
Neither is conserved, because the objects push on each other

items.q: A collision in which the total kinetic energy after is less than before, but the objects do not stick together, is
options: elastic
perfectly inelastic
an explosion
inelastic

items.q: A 1500 kg car moving at 12 m/s rear-ends a 1000. kg car at rest, and they lock bumpers. How fast do they move just after, in m/s?

mistakes.why: Value: that comes from conserving kinetic energy. Locked bumpers make it perfectly inelastic; use momentum.

items.q: A ball of clay and a rubber ball, of equal mass and speed, each hit a block. Which one is more likely to knock the block over?
options: The rubber ball, because a bounce gives a larger impulse
The clay, because it hands its whole energy to the block
Both equally, because they have the same momentum
The clay, because sticking is an elastic collision

items.q: Two identical carts, one moving at v and one at rest, collide on a frictionless track. Which outcome is impossible?
options: The first cart stops and the second moves at v
Both carts move forward at v
They stick and then move together at v/2
The first moves at v/4 and the second at 3v/4

items.q: Two carts on a frictionless track collide and stick together. For the two-cart system, compare just after with just before.
